#4761. Is Yeti’s $200 Camp Blanket Worth It? I Tested It Out for Months to Find Out.

Hint: It low-key might be one of Yeti’s best products.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

YETI IS KNOWN to drop a lot of product. The Austin-based brand emerged as a key player in the cooler category and has since grown immensely, putting out everything from fleeces to outdoor furniture.

The Lowlands Blanket, an durable outdoor blanket, might be a piece that gets overlooked in the brand’s offering. The original came out a few years back but Yeti has added some new colors as well as improvements like the diamond-stitched pattern. It’s waterproof, claims to repel dirt and pet hair, and comes in a host of core and seasonal colors (not to mention two different sizes). As an all-purpose, throw-kind of blanket, it’s meant to be put to use pretty much anywhere, from the back of your car or atop some cold bleachers at the soccer game to the campsite or picnic at the beach or state park.

Do you need one though? That all depends. The $200 blanket proved quite capable during testing, packing down nicely and drying at speed. There are pros and cons to the thing, and it really depends on the lifestyle you’re trying to cater to, not to mention the elements you might be operating under.

While we were sitting on a regular-sized Lowlands Blanket during the summer months (quite literally), packing it to a few outdoor concerts and park picnics, we mostly waited patiently for fall. We wanted to really assess the burly, insulated build of the thing and its waterproofness. We spent several weeks with the blanket in the back of the car, at the ready for everything from dog naps and post-paddle warmups to hangouts near the wet soccer field or full-fledged fall camping trips.

Right out of the gate, this is easily one of the most comfortable outdoor blankets we’ve tested in recent history. Down blankets can offer a similar level of sensory joy but the softness of the topside of this blanket feels like something you’d get draped over the best chair in a ski lodge, right in front of the great room fire. It’s mildly fuzzy on one side and more coarse and rugged on the other.

The seasonal colors really pop and add some flavor while the two sizes of the blanket are actually quite distinct and useful in their own ways. The smaller, about 28-in. by 38-in., is about the size of a dog bed and is (surprise) best for pets—setting up a dry sitting spot for one, or thawing wipe downs after playing in the snow. It does not come with a carrying case but rolls up plenty small and doesn’t necessitate one. The larger (the one we tested), measuring 55-in. by 78-in., is more like a bed topper, great for picnics, topping your camp bed, or just wearing around in the cold.

The corner loops are a nice touch for securing the blanket in blustery conditions and can also be used for hanging or tying down valuables. We even tried hanging it up and utilizing it as a temporary wind barrier during outings that involved occasional sideways rain. We found that it worked well as a barrier during offseason camping trips. In other words, as a comforter of sorts to protect you from dirt or the elements while keeping your base-layers or sheets beneath dry.

Cleaning the thing is pretty simple, whether that be a quick wipe-down to address grass stains and mud or a full machine wash after a weekend camping in the woods. One of the blanket’s biggest merits is its thickness, offering more depth than most at close to a half-inch. You can genuinely feel it too. Often, when you throw a packable blanket atop the grass or the sand at the beach you’re banking on the inherent softness of that natural surface and not getting much else. Not so with the Yeti, as it does afford a true layer of added comfort, one that can easily eat up contours in uneven surfaces or small rocks and sticks.

Yeti tends to follow the go big or go home philosophy, which we’re used to at this point and oftentimes suits the product and its intentions well. At nearly six pounds, it’s admittedly a bit heavy for a blanket. But you can feel instantly where all that weight is going (the ample insulation and reinforced exterior). The weight is not a huge deal, especially if you utilize the packing bag that it comes with, which you can grab by hand or sling over your shoulder. It’s more noticeable if you’re just carrying it about unfolded or rearranging that picnic spread. But, because it translates to more comfort and durability, we’re all for it. Just keep it in mind for towing purposes if you’re looking for something to pack along on a hike, you can find something far lighter.

The internet has alerted us to the possibility of mold if not dried off properly or machine-washed fairly often. While we didn’t experience that, the blanket is thicker and seemingly takes on odors a bit more than some. What’s perhaps more of an issue is the noise, which is only relatively louder than, say, a puffy blanket, which tends to offer a more whispered kind of sound when moving about beneath it. This is probably only a real issue for sensitive sleepers.

For do-it-all blankets built for the outdoors, there are a few alternatives. Rumpl has a line of nimble options that often come in cool patterns. The price is right but you’re generally getting either a mat or a puffy (although you can certainly pair the two up for more waterproofness). They’re billed as weather-resistant and while they look great and feel like snuggling into a zipped sleeping bag, they don’t quite have the waterproof build and toughness of Yeti. However, if you’re after a high warmth-to-weight ratio, it’s tough to go wrong here. Nomadix makes another quality option, a puffer blanket that packs more tightly than most, weighs just two pounds, and is even made with a bunch of recycled material. Yet, if you’re going to be dealing with more than wet grass (e.g. snow) or plan to be in more than low-level precipitation, you’ll want something more substantial.

White Duck Outdoors makes a solid one too in the Trailside Blanket, which comes in under $100, weighs just three pounds, has a streamlined layer of insulation, and smart magnetic closures for when you want to wear it. While a lot of Pendleton’s blankets are form over function, the Oregon brand does make a nice all-weather option in the Roll-Up Blanket, priced comparably to the new Yeti. It does come armed with a weather-resistant nylon side and a soft wool side to hang out on.

For an all-purpose outdoor blanket that can take you from the snowy slopes to the trail and pretty much everywhere in between, this is a tough one to beat. It’s more durable than many we’ve tested, offers more comfort by way of added depth and nicely-stitched insulation, and even fends off pet hair swimmingly. While a great accompaniment to camping adventures, the Lowlands Blanket is also great for elevating the outdoor music festival, throwing atop a damp yard, or lugging to the tailgater (especially in the fall and winter).

This regular size is $200, a fair chunk of change (the small version is $75). And while that’s not cheap, it simply outdoes just about every other blanket in its class. You may not need a heavier, weatherproof blanket if you mostly spend time car camping. But if you want a burly blanket that’s not afraid of the terrain or weather, this one’s for you. Offseason campers are wise to consider it, as are diehard sports fans who like to show up for their team.

#4760. Should Borderline Become Relational Sensitivity Disorder?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

For more than half a century, borderline personality disorder (BPD) has survived an unusual amount of conceptual scrutiny. Initially regarded as a variant of schizophrenia, it has subsequently been reconceptualized by some as a mood disorder, a post-traumatic disorder, or an impulse-control disorder. Others have called for the diagnosis to be abandoned altogether. Each time, the syndrome has proved more durable than its critics expected (Gunderson, 2009). Today, however, the most serious threat to the diagnosis comes from a different direction: the movement toward dimensional models of personality disorder.

ICD-11, the World Health Organization's diagnostic system, has already replaced the traditional personality disorder categories with a single diagnosis rated by severity and described by maladaptive trait domains. Borderline survived only as an optional "borderline pattern" specifier, a concession many regarded as a political compromise. The DSM-5 Alternative Model for Personality Disorders moves in a similar direction. If this trend continues, borderline psychopathology risks being reduced to a configuration of trait scores, despite decades of evidence supporting its validity as a distinct psychiatric syndrome.

Against this backdrop, a group of clinicians, researchers, and people with lived experience in the United Kingdom has launched the Relational Sensitivity Project. Founded by Orestis Zavlis, with Peter Fonagy, Peter Tyrer, Michael Moutoussis, and Lorraine Liu among its founding members, the initiative asks the World Health Organization to remove the borderline pattern specifier from the personality disorders section of ICD-11 and to recognize relational sensitivity disorder as a separate psychiatric diagnosis. It would not be a subtype or modifier of personality disorder.

The proposed criteria will look familiar to anyone who has worked with borderline patients: fear of abandonment, unstable relationships, an unstable sense of self, intense and reactive affect, impulsive efforts to soothe distress, and self-harm. The argument is that these features are neither broad enough nor stable enough to count as personality in the usual sense. They cluster in emotional and relational life, and they frequently remit over time (Zanarini et al., 2012).

It is particularly striking that Tyrer and Fonagy are both involved. Tyrer chaired the working group that developed the dimensional ICD-11 model, while Fonagy, with Anthony Bateman, developed mentalization-based treatment specifically for borderline patients. Their collaboration suggests that the case for preserving borderline psychopathology, even under a different name and classification, is not confined to any one theoretical camp.

Interestingly, the proposal aligns closely with the work of the Harvard psychiatrist John Gunderson, who did more than anyone to establish BPD as a valid and reliable psychiatric diagnosis. Gunderson (1984) believed that the core psychopathology of BPD involved a profound disturbance in interpersonal functioning. Borderline patients are exquisitely sensitive to rejection and abandonment, and their symptoms rise and fall with their perception of the availability and responsiveness of the important people in their lives. He called this interpersonal hypersensitivity (Gunderson & Lyons-Ruth, 2008). "Relational sensitivity" is, in many respects, a new name for Gunderson's central insight.

Late in his career, Gunderson (2013) also argued that BPD should be moved to Axis I of DSM, separating it from the other personality disorders, which he viewed as more amenable to dimensional classification. He proposed the same reclassification for antisocial personality disorder. The Relational Sensitivity Project arrives at much the same conclusion by a different route.

In my forthcoming book, The Borderline Dilemma (Karnac Books), I make a related argument. Psychiatric classification should be guided primarily by the validity of our diagnostic constructs rather than by a priori commitments to either categorical or dimensional models. Some personality disorders are clearly dimensional, but borderline psychopathology has substantially greater empirical support as a distinct psychiatric syndrome than most of the other personality disorders. Although BPD involves underlying personality traits, the disorder cannot be adequately reduced to their combination (Paris, 2007). I am therefore not convinced that BPD belongs among the personality disorders as traditionally conceived.

Where I part company with the proposal is the name. I favor retaining the term borderline, in part because it preserves recognition of the frequent psychotic symptoms that helped define the syndrome. Under interpersonal stress, borderline patients may experience paranoid ideation, dissociation, and hallucinations; one study found a point prevalence of hallucinations of 43% (Niemantsverdriet et al., 2017). Historically, the word borderline reminded clinicians that these patients may temporarily regress to psychotic modes of experience while retaining the capacity to return to intact reality testing.

I am also skeptical that a new name will, by itself, defeat stigma. Stigma attaches less to words than to the conditions they denote, and it tends to migrate to new terminology. What ultimately reduces stigma is better understanding and more effective treatment. If a change is needed, the term originally used by Grinker and colleagues, the borderline syndrome (Grinker et al., 1968), would mark the disorder's distinct status while preserving continuity with more than half a century of research.

Nevertheless, I am sympathetic to the broader nosological argument advanced by Zavlis and colleagues. As dimensional models increasingly reshape personality disorder diagnosis, there is a strong case for preserving borderline psychopathology as a distinct category rather than reducing it to a configuration of maladaptive traits. The specialized treatments that have transformed the outlook for borderline patients, including dialectical behavior therapy, mentalization-based treatment, transference-focused psychotherapy, and good psychiatric management, were developed for a specific syndrome, not for isolated trait dimensions.

Whether it is called borderline personality disorder or relational sensitivity disorder, the more important question is whether the syndrome itself remains recognizable as a coherent and clinically meaningful form of psychopathology. On that question, the Relational Sensitivity Project and I are on the same side.

To learn more about the Relational Sensitivity Project, please visit relational-sensitivity.org.

Grinker, R. R., Sr., Werble, B., & Drye, R. C. (1968). The borderline syndrome: A behavioral study of ego-functions. Basic Books.

Gunderson, J. G. (1984). Borderline personality disorder. American Psychiatric Press.

Gunderson, J. G. (2009). Borderline personality disorder: Ontogeny of a diagnosis. American Journal of Psychiatry, 166(5), 530–539. https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.2009.08121825

Gunderson, J. G. (2013). Seeking clarity for future revisions of the personality disorders in DSM-5. Personality Disorders: Theory, Research, and Treatment, 4(4), 368–376. https://doi.org/10.1037/per0000026

Gunderson, J. G., & Lyons-Ruth, K. (2008). BPD's interpersonal hypersensitivity phenotype: A gene-environment-developmental model. Journal of Personality Disorders, 22(1), 22–41. https://doi.org/10.1521/pedi.2008.22.1.22

Niemantsverdriet, M. B. A., Slotema, C. W., Blom, J. D., Franken, I. H., Hoek, H. W., Sommer, I. E. C., & van der Gaag, M. (2017). Hallucinations in borderline personality disorder: Prevalence, characteristics and associations with comorbid symptoms and disorders. Scientific Reports, 7, Article 13920. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-13108-6

Paris J. (2007). The nature of borderline personality disorder: Multiple dimensions, multiple symptoms, but one category. Journal of Personality Disorders, 21(5), 457–473. https://doi.org/10.1521/pedi.2007.21.5.457

Ruffalo, M. L. (in press). The borderline dilemma. Karnac Books.

Zanarini, M. C., Frankenburg, F. R., Reich, D. B., & Fitzmaurice, G. (2012). Attainment and stability of sustained symptomatic remission and recovery among patients with borderline personality disorder and axis II comparison subjects: A 16-year prospective follow-up study. American Journal of Psychiatry, 169(5), 476–483. https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.2011.11101550

#4759. Here Are the 7 Best Long-Sleeve Shirts for Cold-Weather Workouts

Stay dry, cool, and protected during your workouts with our favorite long-sleeve shirts.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FALL IS HERE, and with it, the chill is starting to hit the air. This change in temperature shifts the spotlight to what we think is the unsung hero of your fall and winter workout wardrobe, especially when it comes to your workouts: the long-sleeve T-shirt.

Whether you’re trying to ward off goosebumps or protect your skin from the sun, long-sleeve shirts are a solid choice for training. Many are made from the same performance fabrics as our favorite workout shirts; they can wick moisture and keep you cooler than a wool layer while offering more coverage than a short-sleeve tee.

Collectively, the Men’s Health editorial team has trained in dozens of long-sleeve shirts and pooled our experience to bring you seven picks for different types of training.

The long-sleeve sibling of our best overall workout shirt also snags the top spot in our roundup of long-sleeve workout shirts. After all, it’s virtually the same shirt, just better suited for fall and winter workouts.

The Strato Tech Tee is among the softest shirts I’ve ever worn, and after a year of consistent use, mine still looks, feels, and performs much like it did during my first week of testing. Its four-way-stretch fabric contributes to its excellent comfort, and despite the shirt’s paper-thin feel, it was surprisingly effective at wicking moisture during our sweatiest workouts.

Because it’s lightweight, keeps sweat at bay, and is versatile enough to double as an everyday shirt, the Strato Tech earns its near-$70 price tag. It’s the kind of staple worth investing in.

The skin-tight fit of compression gear doesn’t appeal to everyone, but compression shirts offer plenty of utility. You can wear one on its own, under a short-sleeve tee for a fall or winter workout, or as a base layer for skiing and hiking.

Dick’s Sporting Goods’ DSG compression crew is a good option for skeptical buyers. It costs $30 per shirt and comes in more than 15 color options. The trade-off for that affordability is slightly less comfort. In particular, the seams that run along the arms can be a little annoying. It also runs a bit longer than I prefer, so I opted to tuck mine in.

Read More: Best Compression Shirts, Tested by Us

Gymshark has cemented itself as a major player in the fitness apparel space, not just because of the quality of its clothing, but also because its marketing and product lines often reflect what the current generation of gymgoers are wearing.

The Power Long Sleeve T-Shirt is a good example. It leans into the current pump-cover trend, where lifters wear oversized layers at the start of a workout and shed them once they’re warmed up and pumped. The Power Tee fits oversized but true to size and keeps the look simple, save for “Gymshark” printed across the back. It also comes in four colors.

Because it’s made from 95% cotton, expect it to hold onto more heat and sweat than a technical training shirt. I wouldn’t reach for it for hard runs or conditioning sessions, but for lifting, it works well either as a standalone shirt or as an extra layer to keep you warm between sets.

When people think of Under Armour, they often think of compression gear, so its HeatGear line—a collection designed to provide coverage while keeping athletes cool—is a natural pick for anyone who wants to keep their arms covered during spring and summer workouts.

Athletes who wear pads, trail runners looking for protection from brush, and even people with sun-sensitive skin can all benefit from the extra coverage. HeatGear fabric is ventilated and described by Under Armour as “ultra-light,” so the shirt offers protection without adding much bulk or warmth. And at $40 with 16 color options, it’s an affordable, versatile choice that works as either a standalone training shirt or a base layer.

Co-owned by Mark Wahlberg, Municipal is a lifestyle and fitness brand that makes gear for activities including training, golf, and running. The Enduro Stretch LS can work as a running shirt, but its minimal branding and simple design make it versatile enough for lifting, errands, or casual wear, too.

It has the hallmarks of a solid workout shirt: super stretch, moisture-wicking fabric, and a lightweight feel, all from a 100% polyester construction. The ribbed cuffs bring a lot more durability to the sleeves and a little style, so that you get more use out of this piece.

Municipal is still a relatively young brand, and the Enduro Stretch LS is only available in three colors, with fewer customer reviews than some of the more established options on this list. At this price, that makes it a slightly less proven pick, but its simple design and performance-focused construction give it plenty of appeal for runners and lifters alike.

If most of your training takes place outside, this is the shirt worth investing in. Ten Thousand—a brand that’s made it onto our best workout shirt and best workout shorts lists—built the Tactical Long Sleeve with sun protection, odor-blocking technology, and micro-mesh fabric designed to help regulate body temperature.

The shirt also uses flatlock seams, which lie flatter against the skin and help reduce irritation while reinforcing high-stress areas. The upper back, or yoke, is reinforced to better withstand ruck sacks, plate carriers, and weighted vests. There are a few trade-offs: It only comes in two colors (black and green), the care instructions are a little finicky, and it costs close to $100.

The Tactical is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that cost more up front but may save you money if it holds up longer than cheaper shirts. And Ten Thousand does have a one-year guarantee on their clothes. That said, not everyone wants to—or can— spend that much on a workout shirt, and you certainly don’t need one this rugged for every outdoor training session.

If you like wearing sleeves year-round, it’s worth investing in a lightweight shirt that keeps you covered without trapping too much heat. Barbell Apparel’s Arid Drop Hem Long Sleeve is made from a blend of bamboo, polyester, and a touch of spandex for added stretch and mobility. Customers describe it as lightweight and flattering, which tracks for a brand that built its name making clothes for people with more athletic builds.

Designed for warm-weather use, the Arid also includes odor control and UV protection, while its looser fit through the torso helps keep the fabric from clinging as you sweat. Aesthetically, it fits in just about anywhere, and its two neutral color options—black and a grayish blue—make it easier to get more mileage out of the hefty price tag.

Most workout shirts are made primarily from synthetic materials such as polyester, nylon, and elastane. These fabrics tend to dry faster than cotton and can be engineered to move moisture away from your skin, which helps keep the shirt from feeling soaked during a workout.

Cotton, by comparison, absorbs and holds onto more moisture, which can leave a shirt feeling heavy and damp and may contribute to chafing or irritation. That doesn’t mean cotton has no place in workout gear. Some shirts blend in a small amount to soften the fabric and improve comfort. An all-cotton shirt may be less appealing for sweaty sessions, but a little cotton in the blend isn’t necessarily a drawback.

Odor control generally comes down to two things: how quickly the fabric dries and whether it has been treated to limit odor-causing bacteria. Moisture-wicking, quick-drying fabrics can help keep sweat from sitting against your skin for as long, but the fabric itself doesn’t automatically prevent odor.

Some manufacturers also treat fibers with antimicrobial technologies designed to slow bacterial growth. Silver, copper, and zinc-based treatments are common examples. Other brands use different chemical or bio-based treatments to achieve a similar effect. If odor control matters to you, look for a specific antimicrobial or anti-odor claim rather than assuming every synthetic shirt has it.

You probably don’t need to obsess over seams, but they’re worth paying attention to if you’re prone to chafing. Look for flatlock seams, which sit flatter and feel less bulky against the skin, as well as thoughtful seam placement in high-friction areas.

The armpit is one of the more annoying places to have bulky stitching, which is why some workout shirts use raglan sleeves. Instead of a traditional sleeve seam that starts at the shoulder, raglan sleeves extend up toward the collar and create diagonal seams across the upper chest and back. That construction can reduce irritation and allow for more freedom of movement.

No. Many long-sleeve workout shirts are lightweight enough to wear comfortably during spring and summer, depending on the temperature and your personal preference.

There are also practical reasons to cover up in warm weather. Long sleeves can help shield your arms from direct sun and offer some protection from rough brush, branches, gravel, and other elements if you train outdoors or spend a lot of time on the trails.

As a fitness writer, personal trainer, and guy who likes to train, I spend a lot of time in workout clothes, usually while lifting or running. I’m fortunate that companies send me samples throughout the year—always with no strings attached—to test, and Men’s Health will occasionally ship specific products to my house for dedicated testing.

Creating this list was a collective effort between the Men’s Health editorial team and me, including Fitness and Reviews Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan. Our standard testing protocol is to wear each shirt for at least two weeks and put it through common exercises like pull-ups, push-ups, and deadlifts. At the time I wrote this article, I was also logging 15 to 25 miles of running per week across the treadmill, road, and local trails, so I rotated several of these shirts through those sessions to see how they held up.

We take notes on each shirt’s style, fit, comfort, price, versatility, and performance, including stretch, moisture management, and breathability. We also pay attention to sizing—whether a shirt fits true to size or runs large or small—and how the fabric holds up after repeated workouts and washes. What we don’t do is chase trends. Our goal is to recommend shirts that perform well now and should still make sense years from now.

Andrew Gutman, NASM-CPT is a journalist with a decade of experience covering fitness and nutrition. His work has been published in Men's Health, Men's Journal, Muscle & Fitness, and Gear Patrol. Outside of writing, Andrew trains in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, helps coach his gym's kickboxing team, and enjoys reading and cooking.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

#4758. Dems introduce new $15,000 EV tax credit bill that has no chance — and that’s a problem

Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) wants to bring back the federal EV tax credit and double it. His new bill, the “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” (H.R. 10881), would offer up to $15,000 on a new electric vehicle and $8,000 on a used one, and it would make both credits permanent.

The problem is that the bill has virtually no chance of becoming law anytime soon. And if EV shoppers start holding out for it, it could end up hurting the market it’s trying to help.

Landsman introduced H.R. 10881 on October 22. It was referred to three House committees (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources), and as of today, it doesn’t have a single cosponsor.

The big change is to the new clean vehicle credit, Section 30D of the tax code. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, the $7,500 credit came in two $3,750 halves: one for meeting critical mineral sourcing requirements and one for battery components. Landsman’s bill doubles each half to $7,500, for a maximum of $15,000.

It also deletes the termination dates. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed the new and used EV credits for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and the home charger credit after June 30, 2026. Striking those dates would revive all three credits with no expiration.

The bill doesn’t touch the rest of 30D. North American final assembly, the $55,000 MSRP cap on cars and $80,000 cap on SUVs, pickups, and vans, and the foreign entity of concern rules all stay. So the full $15,000 would only go to EVs that clear both sourcing tests, which has always been a short list.

The rest of the bill is reports. Commerce would deliver a “Vehicle Choice Report” on vehicle variety and ownership costs, and the Department of Energy would file five years of critical minerals reports.

The most interesting part is a DOE study of “gasoline super-users,” defined as the top 10% of light-duty vehicle owners by gas consumption. The study would map the regions where they’re concentrated and their 100 most-used routes, then track charger availability along those routes every year for five years. Coltura, which backs the bill, says the highest-mileage drivers spend over 10% of household income on fuel.

Republicans control both the House and the Senate, and they’re the ones who just repealed these credits. President Trump signed that repeal.

Even if Democrats flip the House and Senate in next week’s midterms, a bill restoring EV credits would still need to get through a veto. So realistically, nothing like this happens before 2029.

It’s also a rerun. Landsman introduced the exact same “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” as H.R. 10046 on October 25, 2024, 11 days before that year’s election. It got zero cosponsors and died in committee. This version landed 12 days before the November 3 midterms.

This is where the bill can do real damage. EV buyers are extremely sensitive to tax credit timing, and the last year proved it.

When the credit was about to disappear, buyers rushed in, and Q3 2025 became the best quarter ever for US EV sales, with market share topping 10% for the first time. Then the floor dropped out. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 sales fell 63% the month after the credit ended.

The market is only now crawling back. According to Cox Automotive, US EV sales hit 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% from Q2 but still down 39.5% year-over-year, at a 6.4% share of new vehicle sales. Tesla’s Model Y and Model 3 still dominate, but Toyota, Rivian, and Hyundai are growing again.

That recovery is fragile. A headline promising “$15,000 off your next EV” is exactly what makes a shopper on the fence decide to wait a year or two.

And waiting gets you nothing. The new credits would only apply to vehicles placed in service after the bill is enacted, so there’s no retroactive payout for buying now. If you already claimed the credit once, you’d get $0 anyway.

Meanwhile, the deals on the lot are real. Automakers have been cutting prices to make up for the lost credit, like Hyundai, which cut the 2026 Ioniq 5 by nearly $10,000 on some trims.

At Electrek, our position has always been clear: we think EVs are a net positive and ICE vehicles have unpriced externalities. Therefore, we will take whatever we can get to encourage EV sales, but our preferred approach would be a carbon tax on ICE vehicles.

We’ve been clear that policy shapes this market. Killing the $7,500 credit is the main reason US EV sales collapsed. Consumers didn’t suddenly decide they hate EVs. So we’re all for bringing incentives back.

But this bill is messaging. It has zero cosponsors and no CBO score, and it dropped two weeks before an election, just like the identical version two years ago.

They should focus on rooftop and community solar tax credits and initiatives. With rising electric rates, helping people alleviate those would be vastly more popular than EV subsidies.

To be fair, some of it is smart. The lower income caps and the once-per-taxpayer limit go after the most common criticism of the old credit, that it subsidized wealthy households buying their second or third EV. And the “super-user” study is the best idea in the bill. Getting a high-mileage driver out of a gas pickup does far more for fuel costs and emissions than putting a low-mileage commuter in their second Tesla. If Democrats want to rebuild EV policy in 2029, that’s where they should start.

The problem is that people will hear the headline number. If you need a car now and an EV fits your life, buy it now and take the deals that are on the table. Don’t plan your purchase around a bill that has no path to passing for at least two years.

Will Democrats come back with a real, cosponsored EV plan before 2028? I don’t know, but I suspect that the US will continue to fall behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, with or without a tax credit. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. And with lease and PPA options, you can do it with zero upfront cost and start saving immediately. If you want to find the best deal, check out EnergySage. It’s a free service with hundreds of pre-vetted installers competing for your business, so you save 20 to 30% compared to going it alone. No sales calls until you pick an installer. #4757. Puffer Jackets, Wetsuits, Headphones, and More: The Coolest Gear Our Editors Are Testing This Month

Gear that can actually handle colder weather.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Welcome to the MH Gear Report, where Men’s Health gear and tech experts find the coolest new releases in gear, technology, home goods, and more. Plus, some insights into new gear we’ve been testing lately.

THE HOLIDAYS ARE fast approaching, and we’re already prepping for Black Friday and Cyber Monday here at Men’s Health. But that doesn’t mean our gear testing stops. In fact, we’re in a switch right now with the cooler weather and getting to finally test things like puffer jackets, midlayers, and wetsuits.

While we’re always testing products like headphones or running shoes no matter where the calendar is at, these seasonal shifts give us the chance to dig into some other activities and regimens. And then getting to translate all those experiences to you so you know what’s good, what’s not, and what’s just ok.

Nothing finally built a pro-level pair of cans and there’s a lot to love: physical buttons, great battery life (30+ hours), improved active-noise cancelling that’s really good, and the signature transparent look that the brand has become known for. They are a bit heavy (you expect that from pro headphones) and the ear cushioning is slightly less firm than we’d like, but these have been a pair we’re going to keep wearing most days.

The Adios Pro 5 is lighter and more responsive than the Pro 4, and has a reworked upper (that helps create a more locked-in fit) and a new midsole foam formulation that feels closer to firm than cushy. Lots of runners gunning for a race PR will love the Pro 5 for their goal event and their fastest training days.

Read More: Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 5 Review

“I love this lightweight insulated jacket,” Creative Director Jamie Prokell says. “It’s the perfect transitional coat—somewhere between a down puffer and a bomber, the Lapwing looks stylish on its own and provides the right amount of warmth without the bulk.”

Later in the season, its low-profile design also makes it a great liner under a shell. And you can feel good knowing that its REPREVE insulation and recycled performance fabrics work well while also being better for the planet.

Ciele makes more than just running hats, and this pair of run shorts is already a great offering with the 2-in-1 compression-like short underneath and a very light and flowy short on top. But given a more reflective detailing treatment for the Nite Rite capsule, these bad boys are perfect for the shorter days we’re now getting.

The U-zip wetsuit is a fairly new offering from a few brands, and Patagonia’s version is one we’ve just started testing given the season. Like all Patagonia wetsuits, it’s made neoprene-free (which is petroleum-based) with Yulex natural rubber and synthetic rubber. So this easier-to-get-into suit is also a bit better for the planet.

Utilizing Polartec’s Alpha Direct fleece (which was originally developed for U.S. Special Forces), this active quarter zip is built for movement. The weight-to-warmth ratio is serious, and the beauty of the open-mesh fleece fabric is that it’s great at insulating but also at dumping heat when things get too warm. While lots of brands are using this material right now, this is one of the more unique offerings we’ve tried in the QZ (most are hoodies with scuba-style hoods).

While the screenless fitness tracker trend certainly took hold in 2026, there’s still lots of folks who want some screen. The new Fitbit Edge is the successor to the Charge 6 and leans into the design that Fitbit became known for.

Out of nowhere last month, Yeti dropped a performance apparel line made up of four pieces: a down jacket, a rain jacket, a zip-up fleece, and a quarter-zip fleece. It’s a pivot into outdoor apparel we can’t say we expected, but it does make a bit of sense. We’ve just gotten pieces in for testing and plan to have a full review up soon, but these do look and feel the part. Yet they do come with the premium Yeti price tag as well.

Yes, Skechers has made a carbon-plated race shoe and it’s pretty solid. Lightweight at 5.9 oz, the woven jacquard upper is comfy and the closure system allows for a secure fit—it’s also got that slightly off-center lacing to help avoid hot spots on the top of the foot, which I find meaningful. The propulsion from this shoe is pretty decent, without it feeling unnatural. After some speed work, I’ve found the faster the pace the more the shoe settles in for me. I think it might be my pick for a 5K turkey trot later this month.

For guys who run warm (like lots of our editors), The Eight Sleep Pod mattress cover has been a game changer. With its temperature control and sleep tracking, it’s let us create personalized zones that match our physiology. The latest version improves the user experience and comes in at a lower price than past releases, plus it gives you the option to just get a half mattress cover for cheaper (for bachelors) or the full cover.

“I often wear 100% Merino baselayers for training in my garage in winter but they can be a little itchy,” says Executive Editor Ben Court. But as Ben has found out, the Worn 80Hr Tee has the thermal and sweat-wicking qualities of wool but is made from a blend of 85 percent merino, 12 percent nylon, and 3 percent elastane so it's a little softer. Plus, the extra stretch from the elastane means the sleeve fit is more snug and flattering on your biceps.

The Bose Ultra Open Earbuds are still a pair we’re constantly grabbing when we want a reliable, open-ear experience. The brand’s latest open-ear development leans further into the clip style and are truly built for active use. You get an IP54 water-resistance rating (opposed to a lesser IPX4) and physical, tactile buttons that are much easier to utilize when things get sweaty. The biggest appeal is these are $100 less than the Ultra ones, so it’s an easy choice if you’re looking for a pair for running, the gym, or any activity.

By now, it’s well known that Away makes a solid travel suitcase. If you’ve ever rolled a bag over a textured surface while holding coffee in one hand, you know how hard it can be to keep everything moving. Away has perfected the roll, making the walk to the gate feel effortless. “With its latest Series 3 case, the brand has upgraded the experience by adding locking wheels—so there are no more runaway bags while you pay at the counter or riding the tram,” Prokell says. “The internal compression system provides plenty of space and helps everything arrive in the same shape it left.”

The Carry-On Flex fits into nearly every overhead bin, regardless of the plane’s size. But if you usually fly on larger planes—or wear shoes bigger than a size 11—you might want to upgrade to the Bigger Carry-On Flex for a little extra room and a more comfortable fit for your footwear.

#4756. Used EVs are suddenly hot sellers — Here are the top SUVs for under $25,000

Don’t want to pay full price? Used EVs with low miles, like the Hyundai IONIQ 5 and Ford Mustang Mach-E, are selling on the secondhand market for $25,000 or less.

With a flood of electric cars returning from lease this year and soaring gas prices, used EVs are suddenly flying off the lot.

Used EV sales rose to a record 3.3% of total used vehicle sales last month, up from 2.9% in August, according to Cox Automotive.

Used ICE vehicle sales, on the other hand, dropped 4.4% in September as buyers flocked to more efficient options.

As expected, Tesla remains the leading used EV brand, followed by Ford, Chevrolet, Hyundai, and BMW.

By model, the Nissan Ariya led growth, with sales up 42.5% in September, followed by the Chevy Equinox EV (+41.9%), Kia EV9 (+36.2%), and Chevy Blazer EV (+30.2%), while the Ford Mustang Mach-E (+14.7%) and Tesla Model Y (+13.8 %) also saw more demand.

With more options to choose from, which one is best for you? To help you decide, Edmunds, which has tested nearly all of them, put together a list of four top used electric SUVs available for under $25,000.

The first one on the list was the Chevy Equinox EV, or as GM used to call it, “America’s most affordable 315+ range” electric vehicle.

After it arrived in 2024, the Chevy Equinox EV quickly became one of the top-selling electric vehicles in the US outside Tesla, winning over buyers with enough space for a family and plenty of driving range at an affordable price.

The Chevy Equinox EV offers up to 319 miles of EPA-estimated driving range. It’s a great fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that still offers plenty of interior space.

Edmunds says it’s worth upgrading to the 2LT trim, which adds heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, a wireless phone charger, adaptive cruise control, and a 360-degree HD Surround Vision camera system.

Next on the list was the Ford Mustang Mach-E, which has also remained a top seller since it went on sale in 2021.

Ford tapped into its iconic Mustang nameplate to help attract new buyers. The Mustang Mach-E came well equipped with a large 15.5″ infotainment screen with Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto and Ford Co-Pilot360 Assist+.

While the GT is the most fun to drive, Edmunds said the Premium trim may be your best bet. It still offers plenty of performance while adding standard features like heated front seats and a heated steering wheel.

It’s also worth upgrading to the extended-range battery pack, which offers up to 320 miles of range on the Premium RWD model. You should be able to find used 2021 to 2023 Mach-E’s for under $25,000.

Another top-selling electric SUV, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 continues to win over buyers with its bold design, long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior.

Edmunds says plenty of used 2022 to 2024 IONIQ 5s with low mileage are available for under $25,000.

While the base SE Standard Range is the cheapest, it only offers an EPA range of 220 miles. Upgrading to the Extended Range battery, which is used on all other trims, provides up to 303 miles of range.

The Volkswagen ID.4 went on sale in the US in 2021 as one of the earlier mainstream electric SUVs.

It also just happens that many EVs are coming off lease so the inventory is plentiful combined with high gas price. Perfect storm.

It was updated in 2024, but up until the 2023 model year, the VW ID.4 offered an EPA range of up to 275 miles, depending on the configuration.

Finding a low-mileage used 2023 ID.4 shouldn’t be hard, but upgrading to the Pro S trim might be worth it.

Volkswagen updated the 2023 ID.4 with a new 12″ infotainment display and Park Assist Plus. The Pro S trim gained a fixed panoramic roof, V-Tex synthetic leather seating, and a heated steering wheel.

#4755. Pope Leo XIV Diagnosed With Lung Cancer After Surgery to Remove Part of Lung

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer following a successful surgery, the Vatican said.

The Pope, 71, underwent surgery at Agostino Gemelli University Policlinic in Rome on October 13 to remove a nodule from his right lung. This was determined to be pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.

The surgeons removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s lung to “ensure a radical procedure; the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the Director of Vatican Healthcare Services, and Professor Stephano Margaritora, the lead surgeon, in a press release.

“An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations,” they said.

Pope Leo was in the operating room for 3 hours, while the operation itself lasted around 90 minutes.

The doctors noted that it was a successful operation with no complications.

According to Matteo Bruni, the Director of the Holy See Press Office, the Pope asked for dinner after the surgery and spent the evening with his secretaries and other Vatican staff.

In a press release on Wednesday, the Vatican said that the Pope’s postoperative recovery is progressing well.

According to Vatican News, Pope Leo had a calm first night following his surgery.

In the coming days, exams will be conducted on the removed tissue. There has currently been no change in the initially announced week of hospitalization.

On October 14, the Pope underwent blood tests and chest X-rays that were scheduled following his surgery. The results of these tests confirm that his postoperative recovery is progressing as expected, and the values are within a normal range for the type of operation performed.

Pope Leo has also undergone some respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room, the Vatican said.

It has not yet been announced whether he will require any further treatment.

Adenocarcinoma is the most common subtype of lung cancer globally. It accounts for around 40% of all lung cancer diagnoses.

Adenocarcinoma is a type of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), which accounts for about 80–85% of all lung cancers.

Lung adenocarcinoma begins in the epithelial cells that produce mucus. It is the most common type of NSCLC.

Adenocarcinoma can be classified further by the genetic changes driving the tumor. For example, EGFR-positive lung cancer is found more often in people who have never smoked and can often be treated with targeted therapies, which is why biomarker testing of tumor tissue helps guide treatment decisions.

Treatment for NSCLC is generally determined by the stage. However, it typically involves one or a combination of:

Surgery is generally the first step in treatment for this type of lung cancer. The right lung has three lobes, or sections, and the left has two.

A doctor will often remove the entire lobe that has the tumor in order to remove the tumor and improve the outlook.

The body eventually adapts in order to compensate for the loss of function.

According to the American Cancer Society (ACS), for NSCLC that hasn’t spread outside of the lung, the 5-year relative survival rate is 67%.

#4754. The Ability to Imagine Peace

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

The act of dreaming places us squarely in the realm of the unexpected. Falling asleep, we leave a familiar world of work and family to enter a landscape of the unknown. Not only are the settings of dreams unexpected, but in our dreams we often act in ways that come as a complete surprise upon waking. Asleep, we could be playing pickleball with our second-grade teacher, or hopping onstage to jam with a jazz band at a huge stadium.

In waking life, we may have famously frozen back in elementary school when our teacher asked us a question, and we may never have picked up an instrument to play in a band. The feelings in dreams of hitting the ball back this time, however, and the courage to be seen onstage and improvise with a group, are real (Kahn, 2013, Tuan, 2001). This embodied component to dreaming is one way that dreams help us to evolve, expanding our imagination for what is possible. As the “I” of the dream, we have a physical experience that grows our sense of self, enabling us to bring these new awarenesses into waking time (Kahn, 2013).

The expanded imagination that dreams offer extends beyond feelings to that of exploring different outcomes. Being able to respond instead of freezing creates a back-and-forth dialogue; spontaneously leaping onstage, instead of sitting on the sidelines, shows us we have a special sound to share with others.

In dreams we get to experience new ways of approaching current challenges without having to pay a real-life price. We “try out” different scenarios and “run the numbers” on what might work best in our conscious experiences. However, because these dream experiments elicit real feelings, we change in the process—our internal database gets updated, which shifts our waking perspective (Hobson 2014, Thompson, 2025).

Imagining new feelings and scenarios are important components to solving challenges, even if that challenge is a conflict with another person. Once we imagine a new possibility, we can make it tangible to transform our waking time.

I once dreamed I was having a deeply connected, loving conversation with a friend I was fighting with in waking life. Sitting shoulder to shoulder, smiling contentedly at each other, in the dream we not only were talking, but I reached over and took his hand.

Waking up from this dream was a shock. Prior to the dream, I couldn't imagine not being mad at what seemed to be now an ex-friend! But the intense feelings of connection in the dream reminded me that we once were very good friends. Despite the current disagreement, deep down was a real bond that was still present. I realized it was possible to experience these feelings again, and the dream even showed me what needed to happen next.

In the dream, I had reached across the gap to take my friend’s hand. I understood upon waking that each of us had retreated to a silent corner and one of us had to make the first move toward reconciliation. I decided that could be me. I acted on the dream, set up a meeting, and I remained open in our discussion instead of retreating again. We resolved our differences, mostly because I now felt and saw that we could.

Conflicts with others often seem impossible to resolve. They follow a certain pattern that creates a structure, like the gap between me and my friend that the dream brought into focus. This structure lives as an inner image. Once we see it, we can solve it.

A client recently recalled a dream of a seemingly simple lunch with her mother. Seated at a comically small table, the mother makes a comment about the dreamer’s behavior. Suddenly the lunch felt dangerous, and suspicious men began to circle around the table. With increasing fear, she feels like there is no way to break the circle and get out.

With this dream, the construct of the relationship was clear; what wasn’t obvious was how to get out of it. In response, I suggested a waking dream exercise, having her close her eyes, return to the dream, and find a way out. She immediately sees a person pick her up, at which point the entire circle breaks up, and suddenly she is free. She reported: “I had no idea such an ingrained structure could so easily dissolve.”

Experiencing how easily dug-in structures can shift, even in dreamtime, gives us the courage to try out other solutions in waking life. After all, nothing changes until our minds change first.

Dreams can play a significant role in problem solving for our waking lives by opening our imagination to new possibilities. But what about taking that approach to a more global level? Can dreams help us with the challenges we face as a larger community?Consider a recent New York Times podcast interview of Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, president of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). Ms. Egger’s job is to monitor world conflicts, usually in person, and to help negotiate an end to these catastrophic problems. In the interview, she repeatedly states that she believes humans fundamentally do not want conflict. While the interviewer pressed her to comment about the state of the world, implying that the situation overall was perhaps quite dire and maybe even hopeless, Ms. Egger simply and clearly responded by suggesting we start by imagining peace. How often do we approach a disagreement, or think about our communities or world, in terms of peaceful outcomes? Whether personally or professionally, most of us default to a worst-case scenario. And yet, what would happen if we all began to see the possibility of creating peace in the world? How would that change our actions and the way we approach situations? How would that transform our attitudes about other people and ourselves? And most importantly, how would these changes shift outcomes?

Being able to imagine peace is often the first step to making peace. One of the tools for developing that imagination is dreaming. Dreaming reminds us of possibilities, helping us to experience feelings of connection and wholeness so that we remember what is possible and have the blueprint for making it tangible. Dreaming and the imagination are the cornerstones of change.

Hobson, J.A., Hong, C. C.-H, Friston, K.J. (2014) Virtual reality and consciousness inference in dreaming. Frontiers in Psychology. 9 October 2014 vol 5, article 1133.

Kahn, D. (2013) Brain basis of self: self-organization and lessons from dreaming. Frontiers in Psychology. Vol. 4, article 408.

Thompson, E. (2025) Enaction as the bringing forth of worlds. Phenomenology and the Cognitive Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11097-025-10079-2

Tuan, Yi-Fu (2001). Space and Place: The Perspective of Experience. University of Minnesota Press.

#4753. Dutch startup Elysian says electric flight may be closer than you think

They day you get to book an all-electric flight may be closer than you think if Dutch startup Elysian Aircraft gets its way. Their new E9X commercial airliner promises flights that are a whole lot quieter, and at prices that are whole lot less dependent on dumb oil wars.

Aircraft account for more than 2% of global heating when CO₂ and other emissions are taken into account, with the share considerably higher in wealthy countries, according to data cited by climate campaign group Stay Grounded. Elysian Aircraft is keenly aware of the industry’s climate impact, and they believe their planned full-size electric airliner will be perfectly positioned to make a dramatic difference.

“By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometers and eventually 1,000 kilometers you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Elysian co-founder Daniel Jacobson told EuroNews. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”

At the core of those ambitious emission-reduction goals is the Elysian E9X aircraft. Designed in collaboration with aerospace researchers at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), the E9X packs its oversized wings with modular battery packs, sending power to six propellers driven by electric motors.

Specs on those haven’t been revealed, but the E9X is designed to carry up to 100 passengers up to 1,000 km (~620 miles) from where they started. Elysian says that’s enough range to handle nearly 50% of scheduled commercial passenger flights worldwide and potentially eliminate 20% of total in-flight emissions when the plane enters service in 2034.

That said, the E9X is far more than “just a concept,” and Elysian has completed its second conceptual design review and flown a scaled demonstrator in concert with Germany’s DLR aerospace research center, demonstrating how its unique battery packaging solutions address the challenges of integrating heavy battery packs into an aircraft’s wings (where fuel is traditionally stored).

It’s interesting to see all the comments that point out the difficulties and problems associated with the introduction of battery powered aircraft into the mainstream industry. What none of them address is the industry’s obsession with cutting their operating costs no matter what pain passengers and flight crews must endure. My bet is if the airlines can save money by converting to battery powered aircraft—there are NO obstacles that will stop them from doing it. Battery electric aircraft may reduce operating costs by thousands of dollars per flight. That alone tells me that they will be flying passengers as soon as possible.

The company is also working with airline partners KLM and Transavia to explore the operational and commercial requirements for putting electric airliners into service, with aircraft lessor TrueNoord investigating how the E9X could be financed and supported commercially.

#4752. BYD now has 1.02 million workers, more than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla combined

BYD now has more than 1.02 million employees, according to chairman Wang Chuanfu. That’s more people than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla employ combined.

And it’s a big jump from the start of the year. BYD reported about 869,600 employees at the end of 2025, which means the Chinese automaker has added roughly 150,000 people in 10 months while its vehicle sales are down.

Roughly 960,000 of BYD’s people work in China and about 60,000 work abroad. Up to 120,000 of them are R&D engineers, according to Wang, who shared the figures on stage Wednesday at the China Society of Automotive Engineers’ (CSAE) 33rd annual conference. Their work covers battery cells, motors, electronic controls, and semiconductors.

Wang credits vertical integration for that scale. In his telling, keeping batteries, chips, and motors in-house is what took BYD from a battery maker founded in 1994 to the world’s top-selling new energy vehicle brand several years running. He called the company’s rise a microcosm of China’s auto industry going from follower to leader.

BYD’s workforce has been all over the place in the last few years.

The company had about 570,100 employees at the end of 2022 and 703,500 at the end of 2023. Then it went on a hiring spree. We reported in September 2024 that BYD had passed 900,000 employees and claimed the largest R&D workforce of any automaker, with over 110,000 engineers. It ended 2024 with 968,900 people.

Then came the first big cut. BYD’s 2025 annual report showed roughly 869,600 employees at year-end, a drop of about 99,000, mostly in frontline production jobs.

Now it’s back over a million. Data compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence put BYD at 911,900 employees at the end of June, so the company added more than 100,000 people in about four months.

The gap with legacy automakers is massive. Volkswagen Group, which counts its Chinese joint ventures, reported 662,942 employees at the end of 2025. Toyota had 390,927 as of March 31, 2026, and Stellantis had 258,668 at the end of last year.

In the US, Ford ended 2025 with 169,000 employees and GM with 156,000. Tesla reported a worldwide headcount of 134,785 in its latest 10-K.

Add up Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla and you get about 851,000 people. BYD has roughly 170,000 more than that.

But headcount isn’t output. If you divide 2025 global vehicle sales by year-end workforce, BYD comes out far behind:

BYD sold about 4.6 million vehicles last year with 869,600 employees, or 5.3 vehicles per worker. Tesla delivered 1,636,129 vehicles with 134,785 people, about 12 per worker, and Volkswagen Group was at about 13.5. Toyota, with 11.3 million group sales including Daihatsu and Hino, got roughly 29 vehicles out of each employee.

There’s a catch, and it’s a big one. BYD’s headcount isn’t only a car company’s headcount. It includes BYD Electronic, its majority-owned contract manufacturer that assembles devices for other brands and reported 165,000 employees of its own at the end of 2025. It also covers BYD’s battery business, which supplies other automakers, plus its in-house chips, motors, energy storage, and rail transit operations.

In short, BYD’s vertical integration largely drives its high headcount.

BYD sold 3,131,576 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, down 3.9% year-over-year. September was its best month of the year at 463,561 units, but the company has been stuck in a brutal price war at home and is losing ground to rivals like Geely and Leapmotor. Its first-half revenue (344.8 billion yuan) and net profit (12.3 billion yuan) were both down year-over-year.

All of the growth is overseas. BYD’s international sales hit 1,342,960 units through September, up 92.7%, and they now make up about 43% of its total volume. That’s on top of BYD beating Tesla on pure EV deliveries again in Q2.

Yet only 60,000 of its 1.02 million workers are based outside China. That’s about 6%. So BYD is still building nearly everything at home and shipping it out, even as its factories in Thailand, Brazil, and Hungary come online.

The 1.02 million number makes for a great headline, but we wouldn’t read it as a sign of strength on its own.

BYD doesn't just make cars. It makes a lot of battery and other parts that go into other things such as other automaker's EVs.

It is automakers, auto supplier, battery makers, electronic contract manufacturer all merged into one.

Remember GM used to make refrigerators and satellites in addition to cars at one point.

BYD’s whole model is to make almost everything itself: cells, chips, motors, seats, and a lot more. That’s a big reason it can sell a Seagull for around $10,000 in China and still make money. But it’s a labor-heavy model, and it works because Chinese factory labor is relatively cheap and plentiful. Toyota gets more than five times as many cars out of each employee. Tesla gets more than twice as many.

The problem is that BYD’s growth is now outside China, and that’s where this model gets tested. Only 6% of its workforce is abroad, yet 43% of its sales are. Tariffs in Europe, Brazil, Mexico, and elsewhere are pushing BYD to build locally, but a factory in Hungary or Brazil won’t necessarily produce the same.

The number that should worry legacy automakers is the 120,000 engineers. That’s almost as many people as Tesla employs in total, all working on product.

#4751. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Not Be Linked to Colorectal Cancer

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Ultra-processed foods as a group do not increase the risk of colorectal cancer, according to a new study.

Researchers from the National Cancer Institute (NCI) report that they found no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and colorectal cancer incidence among the more than 400,000 adults they studied.

They said their findings are important because ultra-processed foods now account for more than half of adults’ energy intake in the United States. They published their research on October 15 in PLOS Medicine.

The study comes amid recent research that has connected ultra-processed foods to an increased risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, and obesity.

However, the link between colorectal cancer and ultra-processed foods has been less clear.

A 2025 study reported that ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of colorectal cancer in females under 50.

A 2022 study found that males who consumed high rates of ultra-processed foods had a higher risk of developing colorectal cancer.

NCI scientists noted in their new study that ultra-processed products represent a wide range of foods.

They pointed out that foods such as whole grains and dairy products were associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer among study participants, while foods such as processed meats were associated with a higher risk.

“We did not observe an association between total ultra-processed food (UPF) intake and colorectal cancer incidence,” said Erikka Loftfield, PhD, a former investigator with the NCI, in a news release. “However, when we looked at food groups, like whole grains, dairy, and meat, by UPF or non-UPF source, we found that associations were in line with current dietary guidance for colorectal cancer prevention.”

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the NCI scientists appear to be on the right track.

“While the study did not find that overall ultra-processed food intake was associated with colorectal cancer risk, the findings suggest that simply classifying foods by their level of processing may not tell the whole story,” said Marissa Shams-White, PhD, a senior principal scientist in population science at the American Cancer Society.

“One of the challenges with studying ultra-processed foods is that the category includes a very wide range of foods and beverages, and we don’t yet know whether they all relate to colorectal cancer risk in the same way,” she added.

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, agrees.

“Just because it is ultra-processed doesn’t mean it is inherently bad or good for you,” he said. “The source of the food and the additives like preservatives, flavorings, sugars, and pigments that are added to increase palatability probably play a much larger role in increasing cancer risk.”

“A whole grain cereal and a hot dog are both UPF, but they push risk in opposite directions,” Thanki noted.

In their study, the National Cancer Institute researchers analyzed data from 461,682 adults aged 50 to 71 years who enrolled in the NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study between 1995 and 1996.

The participants recorded their eating habits using a food frequency questionnaire. Researchers then used that data to estimate each person’s intake of ultra-processed foods. The median consumption of ultra-processed foods among participants was 43% of daily median intake.

The participants were then followed until 2018, for a median of nearly 19 years. The scientists reported that 10,075 cases of colorectal adenocarcinoma were diagnosed during that period.

The researchers reported no association between overall intake of ultra-processed foods and the incidence of colorectal cancer.

However, they said their findings varied by food type. Higher intake of whole grains, fiber, dairy products, and calcium derived from UPF sources was associated with lower colorectal cancer incidence, while meat from UPF sources was associated with higher incidence.

Researchers also found that replacing 10% of gram weight from UPF intake with minimally processed foods was associated with a 2% lower incidence of CRC.

The researchers acknowledged limitations to their study.

They noted that the participants were primarily older, white Americans. In addition, UPF intake was only measured once at the beginning of the study period, so the findings cannot account for changes in eating habits or the increasing availability of ultra-processed foods.

Nonetheless, Ashkan Farhadi, MD, a gastroenterologist at MemorialCare Orange Coast Medical Center in California, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he found the results “very interesting.”

“The definition of ultra-processed foods is so broad,” he told Healthline. “It’s important to designate what type of ultra-processed foods you’re talking about.”

“You shouldn’t just go by whether a food is designated as ultra-processed,” Farhadi added. “You should go by what’s on the [ingredient] label.”

Shams-White shared a similar approach. “When it comes to diet, it is important to follow an overall healthy dietary pattern,” she told Healthline. “Emphasize a variety of fruits and vegetables and whole grains and limit red and processed meats, sugar-sweetened beverages, ultra-processed foods, and refined grain products.”

“Eating a diet rich in fiber and whole grains, dairy and calcium, and limiting processed and red meat and alcohol is what really reduces your risk of developing cancer,” added Thanki.

The American Cancer Society estimates there will be about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer and nearly 50,000 new cases of rectal cancer in the United States in 2026.

The incidence rate is slightly higher in men than in females.

The organization reports that the rate of colorectal cancer cases in the United States has declined since the mid-1980s, but they note that most of that decrease has occurred in older adults.

The incidence rate among people under 50 increased by nearly 3% from 2013 to 2022. Colorectal cancer is now the leading cause of death from cancer for U.S. adults under the age of 50.

Colorectal cancer occurs when cells in the large intestine grow out of control. About 70% of cases begin in the colon.

There are a number of symptoms of colorectal cancer. Some of the common ones include:

Diet is considered one of the risk factors for colorectal cancer. However, there are other considerations.

Farhadi said genetics, obesity, smoking, alcohol consumption, and a sedentary lifestyle can also increase a person’s risk of developing colorectal cancer.

Shams-White noted that the American Cancer Society Guideline for Diet and Physical Activity for Cancer Prevention recommended achieving and maintaining a healthy weight, being physically active, following a healthy eating pattern, and avoiding alcohol and tobacco.

Thanki points out that there are risk factors for colorectal cancer that can be modified and others that can’t.

“Among non-modifiable factors, the biggest are age, a personal or family history of colorectal cancer or advanced polyps, inherited syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, and longstanding inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s colitis),” he told Healthline.

“On the modifiable side, the evidence is strongest for obesity, physical inactivity, smoking, alcohol, and diets high in red and processed meat and low in fiber, whole grains, and calcium,” he added.

Colorectal cancer treatment outcomes improve if the disease is caught at an early stage. The 5-year relative survival for localized colorectal cancer is 91.3%. The 5-year relative survival rate for colorectal cancer caught at various stages, including cancer that has spread, is 65.4%.

Shams-White points out that the American Cancer Society Colorectal Cancer Guidelines recommend that people at average risk of colorectal cancer start getting screened at age 45.

“Screening can help prevent cancer by finding abnormal cells and polyps so they can be removed before they can become colorectal cancer, as well as detect cancer at an earlier stage,” she said.

Thanki had similar advice. “Get screened starting at 45, or earlier if you have a family history or other risk factors, because colonoscopies can prevent cancer by removing polyps,” he said. “And never ignore symptoms like rectal bleeding or a change in bowel habits at any age.”

#4750. When one door closes: Polestar 2 production ends, and epic EV deals

Forget about the 600+ hp hybrid-powered Polestar 1 supercoupe; the car that established Polestar as a standalone brand was the 2. As the brand pulls out of the US and shifts its focus to the rest of the world, it’s time to look back at the EV that helped define Polestar, along with a look around at some of the best EV deals of all time.

A number of European news sites (including Electrive and TV2 Broom) are reporting that the last new Polestar 2 has rolled off the company’s Luqiao assembly line, with more than 200,000 of the all-electric sedan/hatchbacks built in China since the electric sedan launched in 2020. And, while the company hasn’t confirmed that with any sort of official announcement, the news jives with the company’s previously announced plans to release an updated Polestar 2 in 2027, followed by an all-new Polestar 7 SUV that’s set to follow in early 2028.

With the brand set to pull out of the US after the Trump Administration’s Commerce Department declined to grant it authorization under the Connected Vehicle Rule earlier this year, it might at first seem like that US Polestar fans will miss out on that freshened 2, whatever shape it takes – but don’t lose hope, yet.

First shown in 2016, the original Volvo Concept 40.2 was supposed to be a new, entry-level sedan for the now Geely-owned Volvo, which was in the process of separating itself from Ford ownership and the Focus-based C30 coupe and S40/V50 sedan and wagons. And a fine entry-level Volvo it would have been, too, if Tesla’s share price hadn’t made it worth more than the next five most valuable car companies combined.

See, once Tesla (or, more to the point, $TSLA) did that, every carmaker in the world figured the stock market would bless them with billions, too, and started announcing plans to go all electric, right now. Volvo parent company Geely, however, decided they’d fast-track the process, taking the next two Volvo models in their pipeline (the C90 coupe version of the S90 sedan and the C40 sedan previewed by the Concept 40.2) and made them Polestars.

A SPAC merger later, and Polestar was spun off as not only its own brand, but its own, largely Chinese-owned company – which brings us to where we are now.

In the US the Polestar 3 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) SUV starts at something like $67,500 and offers a 111 kWh battery pack good for an EPA-rated range of up to 350 miles. The top-shelf Performance-spec Polestar 3, meanwhile, offers an all-wheel-drive dual-motor setup that Polestar rates at 380 kW (~517 hp) that will launch you across suburbia with a 0–60 mph time in the 4 second range, albeit with slightly less range than the base model … but that $67,500 price is really more of a suggestion these days.

Polestar is offering a $23,000 discount on the 3 and a $25,000, rebate, market adjustment or whatever on the 4. That means that you can get a brand new Polestar 3 or 4 with Chinese EV tech and more than a little bit of Volvo safety baked in for a dramatically reduced price. If you pick the right one at the right dealer, probably for less than $40,000.

One of the best looking cars from the last decade… the 2024+ RWD is such a great value…. I got one myself a year ago for $28k with 5k on the odometer.

As for the 2, I have a bit of a personal connection to that one. My son picked up a 19,000 mile 2024 Polestar 2 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) in Glacier for under $22K, which is an absolutely shocking price for a fast, capable sporty sedan hatchback that isn’t just a worthy successor to the S40 it was meant to replace, but a solid foundation for an EV brand that got wrapped up in politics.
