#4749. Can L-Theanine Supplements Actually Help You Relax and Focus?

The science isn’t as clear as supplement ads suggest.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

A SUPPLEMENT THAT helps you relax and focus sounds like a no-brainer. Some supplement companies are suggesting that L-theanine is your answer. True, dietitians don’t exactly hate this supplement. There are some reasons to suggest L-theanine could do all the above to a certain degree. But there’s a significantly cheaper alternative everyone keeps overlooking. More on that below.

L-THEANINE IS A compound found in tea that allegedly helps you relax and focus.

“Have a demanding task at work late in the day but don't want coffee jitters? Tea's combination of caffeine and L-theanine can give you a calm yet alert mental state that could help boost productivity and effectiveness,” says Kate Ingram, MPH, RD, citing a popular study on caffeine and L-theanine published in Cureus. In supplement form, L-theanine typically has about 200 mg per serving. For context, that’s quite a bit more than the standard 6 milligrams or so in a cup of tea.

L-THEANINE HAS A rare ability to pass through the blood-brain barrier. This semipermeable barricade protects your brain from toxins and other dangerous substances. Not all medications and supplements can safely pass through and affect the brain.

Since L-theanine can pass through to the brain, companies have marketed the compound as a supplement for peak cognitive performance. There’s some science to suggest brain benefits.

In clinical trials, 100 to 400 milligrams of L-theanine produced a “small but statistically significant” improvement in tasks involving visual attention. When paired with caffeine, people also showed greater cognitive performance than without. The cognitive benefits of L-theanine may even show up after a single dose. People who took one 200-milligram dose 30 to 60 minutes before a cognitive test showed higher scores in attention.

Like a good cup of tea, an L-theanine supplement may reduce anxiety and stress. One review suggested 200 to 400 milligrams of L-theanine could calm people who regularly encounter stressful situations.

Researchers decades ago also suggested that people who supplement with L-theanine may sleep more soundly and potentially stave off mental decline. “But the key word is suggest,” says dietitian Perri Halperin, RD. In recent years, scientists reviewing claims of L-theanine increasing alpha waves in the brain to improve sleep quality have found that “findings are often inconsistent.”

One review suggested that L-theanine supplementation could help immune system function—in livestock. There are also studies finding evidence that L-theanine helped to reduce the risk of cancer. Again, in animals only. No supplement has yet been proven to boost immunity in people.

“L-THEANINE IS GENERALLY recognized as safe; however, it is always best to consult your healthcare provider before starting any supplement,” says Ingram. This is especially the case if you have underlying health conditions or are taking other medications. L-theanine supplements could interact with some anti-anxiety, blood-pressure, and sleep meds. Side effects include headaches, dizziness, nausea, and jitteriness.

AS INGRAM PUTS it, “why start a supplement when you can just have a cup of tea?” Plus, with tea you have so many other health benefits such as its potential to improve gut health, promote weight loss, and protect you against chronic disease, Ingram says.

Bottom line: You might get a more set dose of L-theanine if you take it in supplement form, but you'll be paying a lot for something you can get from just brewing a cup of tea. "Tea is certainly a cost-effective way to give it a try,” Ingram says. And, as always, talk to your doctor or a registered dietitian before beginning any type of supplement to ensure that it's something that will work best for you.

#4748. The Woman Who Said Yes While Shaking Her Head No

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

Early on in my career, I was a research manager working on consumer health products for a pharmaceutical company. Part of my job was to develop ideas for new products by testing them in large quantitative surveys to forecast sales. We showed respondents product descriptions I had painstakingly written and asked how likely they would be to buy it.

We tabulated the results to the decimal point, giving the data an aura of accuracy. But there was one problem. What people said in surveys didn’t reliably predict what they bought in market.

I came across a clue as to why sitting behind a two-way mirror. The focus group moderator was reading a product concept we tested in an earlier survey. She asked: “If this was available, would you buy it?” Without hesitating, a woman across the table clearly said yes, while her head was already shaking no.

The woman herself and the moderator didn’t notice. And we all tallied a yes in the backroom.

But her words just didn’t match her gesture. This doesn’t mean a headshake is the same thing as a lie detector. I wasn’t sure what she might do later. But I knew at that time that her answer was less settled than she made it sound.

From then on, I would note verbal and nonverbal responses, and I kept seeing the same split. A yes would arrive with a wince, eye roll, or furrowed brow. Sometimes they would say deadpan they are excited to buy. I would ask them to write down their reasons. The written words seemed well-reasoned and coherent. Over time, the unspoken reactions helped explain what my self-reported surveys were missing. It’s not like the words were useless. But they weren’t the clear window into behavior that the market research industry was built on.

I also had been assuming that honest people could explain their answers. But I started doubting that, and it changed my career path. The pharmaceutical company offered me a paid executive MBA at Columbia. I asked if I could get a degree in psychology. They said no, so I said no. I left to work at a qualitative research firm conducting focus groups and in-depth interviews. The answers weren’t in my spreadsheets, so I’d rather be in the room with people, so I could see the real story show up before the words.

Years later, I found a different kind of research and an aha moment that helped explain the “say versus do gap” that had undermined my earlier self-reported quantitative forecasts.

Neuroscientist Michael Gazzaniga conducted fascinating studies on patients whose corpus callosum, the fibers connecting the two hemispheres of the brain, had been cut to control severe epilepsy. The surgery sharply limited communication between hemispheres, which allowed him to show patients information to one side of the brain without the other side seeing it.

A patient was shown the word “walk” to their right hemisphere and he got up and began walking and the experimenter asked him why. The left hemisphere, which controls speech, hadn’t seen the instruction, so the honest answer should have been "I don’t know." But instead, he said something completely sincere: "I was thirsty and wanted a drink."

Gazzaniga called this left hemisphere function the interpreter: a process that takes something we just did and creates the most coherent explanation based upon whatever information is available.

The woman behind the glass wasn’t a split-brain patient. Her hemispheres communicated normally. We can’t compare the two research studies literally. But what she did share with split-brain patients was the gap: a fluent verbal response that didn’t match her actions. People with intact brains base their explanations on much more information and they often get it right. But Gazzaniga argues that the interpreter is not just a quirk from surgery but something all our brains do as we attempt to make our experiences feel unified and our actions seem like our own doing. The surgery simply made the interpreter more visible; by cutting off information we would normally use.

You can see this in people with normal brains. Researchers at Lund University in Sweden conducted an experiment that let people in a supermarket taste jam. Shoppers were asked which jam they preferred and then asked to taste it a second time. But the experimenters secretly swapped out their preferred jam with another. Most of the participants didn’t even notice the swap, and when asked to describe why they preferred it, they easily explained why, even though they had just rejected it. Despite their brain being fully intact, their reasons seemed like honest reports when they may have been made up.

Have you ever bought something on a whim? You can probably think of a reason why easily. But here’s a harder question: How do you know that is the real reason? Maybe the answer arrived later based on what you know about the product, the moment you bought it, and the person you believe yourself to be?

Or how about bigger decisions, like the job that felt right, the person you just met that you trusted, or that comment from your loved one that made you snap, only to explain it after as: I was just having a bad day. I’m not saying your explanations are fictitious. But maybe it was the simplest story you could put together on such short notice, while leaving out a deeper feeling of being dismissed by them, or some other worry you felt but hadn’t yet named.

Your reasons are not necessarily lies. But alone they’re incomplete. Sometimes there’s a story, and then there’s the real story. When you close a conversation with a quick confident answer you miss an opportunity to dig deeper for a question that deserves to stay open a little longer.

If you ever find yourself doing something surprising, remember your first explanation is just the start not the verdict. Think about what was happening right before and try to parse out if you were moving away or toward something. We tend to avoid bad feelings rather than try to get what we want. We choose a more expensive bottle to avoid looking cheap, agree with someone to avoid a fight, or put off doing something because we fear what might happen. Those reasons are usually not the first things to come to mind. Make sure to check if your story fits everything, not just the things you noticed.

I never learned what that woman finally did. She said yes, but her body said no. And while both responses came from her, neither told the whole story.

Your explanation may be sincere, but it also might be incomplete.

Gazzaniga, M. S. (1998, July 7). Cognitive neuroscientist Michael Gazzaniga on brain hemispheres and behavior [Interview transcript]. Fresh Air Archive: Interviews with Terry Gross. https://freshairarchive.org/segments/cognitive-neuroscientist-michael-gazzaniga-brain-hemispheres-and-behavior

Gazzaniga, M. S. (2011). Who’s in charge? Free will and the science of the brain. Ecco.

Hall, L., Johansson, P., Tärning, B., Sikström, S., & Deutgen, T. (2010). Magic at the marketplace: Choice blindness for the taste of jam and the smell of tea. Cognition, 117(1), 54–61. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cognition.2010.06.010

#4747. New Trek e-bike is first to get Bosch’s new motor with a major power upgrade

Trek is getting a head start on the competition with the latest version of its Marlin+ electric mountain bike, becoming the first North American bicycle manufacturer to feature Bosch’s newly upgraded Active Line Plus motor.

The updated drive system brings more power, less weight, and a smaller footprint to Trek’s approachable electric mountain bike platform, helping make the Marlin+ 6 Gen 2 an even more compelling option for riders who want a capable e-bike without necessarily stepping up to a full-blown, high-performance electric mountain bike.

The Trek Marlin+ has traditionally occupied an interesting Goldilocks position in the company’s electric mountain bike lineup. It’s designed to offer the versatility of a trail-capable eMTB while remaining practical enough for everyday recreational riding, commuting, and exploring gravel paths.

In other words, it’s the kind of electric mountain bike that doesn’t require you to be an actual mountain biker to enjoy it.

And the new Bosch motor seems particularly well suited to that mission.

The biggest upgrade comes courtesy of Bosch’s new-generation Active Line Plus motor, which now offers up to 600 watts of power and 60 Nm of torque.

That’s paired with up to 340% pedal assistance, giving riders a substantial boost when accelerating or tackling climbs.

Despite the improved performance, Bosch has actually managed to shrink the motor. A redesigned two-stage gearbox reduces its volume by 17% while shaving approximately 1.1 lb (0.5 kg) from the previous generation.

The new motor weighs just around 6 lb (2.7 kg), helping manufacturers like Trek build lighter, more streamlined electric bicycles.

Bosch has also focused on improving the riding experience, with updated sensors and software designed to provide smoother, more natural-feeling assistance. Specially machined gears help make the motor virtually silent, while improved sealing and bearings are designed to withstand riding in all weather conditions.

The motor provides pedal assistance up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in the US, making it a Class 1 e-bike without a throttle. With a launch price of US $2,999, it’s also one of the more affordable options in Trek’s lineup.

For a bike like the Marlin+, that combination of moderate weight, smooth assistance, and plenty of usable power could be more important than chasing the enormous torque figures found on increasingly powerful premium eMTBs.

The new motor isn’t the only addition to Bosch’s electric bicycle ecosystem this fall.

The company has also unveiled its new Intuvia 200 display, featuring a 2.4-inch grayscale screen designed to remain readable in bright sunlight. It’s joined by a redesigned LED Controller that’s approximately 65% smaller than the previous LED Remote, offering five thumb-operated buttons and a USB-C charging port.

Bosch is also expanding its theft protection technology with an updated ConnectModule that uses Bluetooth Low Energy alongside GPS and cellular connectivity to help locate stolen e-bikes within a few yards, including in areas where GPS reception is poor.

Perhaps most interesting for long-distance riders is the new PowerTube 720 battery, which packs 720 Wh of capacity into a compact package weighing just 8.6 lb (3.9 kg). Bosch claims up to 115 miles (185 km) of range under favorable conditions on compatible touring e-bikes.

Those additional products are part of Bosch’s broader smart system updates, though Trek hasn’t confirmed which, if any, will be included on the updated Marlin+.

With Bosch supplying drive systems to a large number of e-bike makers worldwide, these upgrades will likely find their way onto plenty of other electric bicycles in the coming months.

But for now, Trek gets the distinction of being first in North America to bring the new Active Line Plus motor to riders.

#4746. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: What Breast Cancer Patients Need When Treatment Ends

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Supporting your health & well-being at every stage of your breast cancer journey

Resources to support your emotional health and well-being

Tips for nourishing your body and mind while living with breast cancer

Navigating your next steps after diagnosis

A guide to medications, treatments, and procedures for breast cancer

Guide to symptoms, tests, and screenings for early detection

Resources to support you during remission or recurrence

Breast cancer awareness has never been higher. Every October, the world turns pink and the key messages—that early diagnosis saves lives and that knowing the risk factors reduces the risk—are hard to miss.

Breast cancer remains the leading cause of cancer death amongst women in most countries, with an estimated 694,000 deaths annually and around 8.2 million women globally living with a breast cancer diagnosis, according to 2024 data from the World Health Organization (WHO)’s Global Health Observatory.

But when October ends, and the wall-to-wall campaigns move on, what has awareness actually changed for those impacted by breast cancer?

For Marisa Weiss, MD, the answer is that there is always more to be done, and she’s uniquely placed to hold that view.

Dr. Weiss has treated breast cancer patients for more than 30 years. In 2000, she founded Breastcancer.org, a not-for-profit that provides expert-reviewed medical and lifestyle information on breast health and breast cancer to millions of people globally.

Sixteen years ago, she was diagnosed with stage 1 breast cancer, becoming, in her own words, a “dual citizen” in that moment, with lived experience on both sides of the doctor’s desk.

I had the pleasure of sitting down with Dr. Weiss as part of Healthline’s Breast Cancer Awareness Month coverage to talk about how awareness has changed care for the better for millions of people around the world, but why critical gaps remain, and how access to trusted information and community can help close those gaps.

“It’s good that awareness is high, but knowledge remains low,” she said. The misconception she sees most is the belief that breast cancer is something that happens to other families.

“Most people think they’re off the hook because it doesn’t run in their family,” Dr. Weiss explained. In fact, 85%-90% of people who get breast cancer have no known family history and no known gene in the family, “so we’re all at risk,” she warns.

For most, a diagnosis arrives as a shock. “They’re completely surprised, flattened by it. Their life is upside down, and they scramble to find what they need to know,” Dr. Weiss noted.

That aftershock caused by a diagnosis is at the core of why Breastcancer.org exists. Because the person whose life is at stake is increasingly expected to direct their own care and advocate for their needs, access to accurate and empowering information is critical in that process. “Decisions aren’t being made around the patient and for the patient in a bubble,” Dr. Weiss said. “Decision-making is supposed to be shared.”

With appointments hard to get and clinicians stretched, she said patients have to do more of the work.

In practice, Dr. Weiss says that means preparing by writing down your family history on both sides and making sure your care team knows who you are. “What’s important to you? Who’s in your life? Do you want more children? Are you planning a vacation? All those decisions can have an impact on the care you receive.”

Where Dr. Weiss sees the widest gap is after treatment ends. Speaking from personal experience, she said: “I had the best care possible, and there were still gaps. You can find yourself alone with lots of questions and fears.”

Understandably, a great deal of focus and attention is centered on diagnosis and treatment, she said. Then it stops. “When your life is supposed to go back to normal, it never does. You have to find a new normal. That quiet phase can be really lonely and difficult.”

For Dr. Weiss, the questions that fill that silence are often as practical as they are emotional: “How do I know my treatment is working? How do I tell leftover side effects from new ones? How do I go back to work, and who do I tell? How do I talk to my kids? What about that new treatment I heard about on TV last night?”

That post-treatment period can also be the first time anyone has really had a chance to stop, take stock, and start asking “what next?”

“You might think, what happened to me? Who do I want to be moving forward? How do I have a long life full of wonderful things, and remain as independent as possible?”

Some of what patients do post-care never reaches their doctor at all, with Dr. Weiss pointing to a growing amount of personal care happening outside the hospital: GLP-1s, peptides, hormonal therapies, supplements, medical cannabis, to name a few. Breastcancer.org’s annual Pulse survey shows that people reported being interested in all of those things and more, and that they tend to learn about them online rather than risk the stigma of bringing them up with their doctors.

“They don’t really trust that their doctor knows much about these things,” she said, “and they don’t want a conversation that makes them feel judged. Some patients worry about what ends up in their medical record and then everyone’s going to know.”

Dr. Weiss says the stakes are real, because some of those choices can interact with cancer medications with potential for adverse or unexpected side effects. “That is why people turn to Breastcancer.org with questions that are personal, private, and important, including “what do I need to share with my doctor, and who’s on a need-to-know basis?”

Peer communities fill part of that gap. “Breastcancer.org’s members share medical information, tips, and practical advice with people who have just had the call, or are about to start treatment and don’t know what to expect,” Dr. Weiss shared, and said that while she values that kind of support system hugely, it does come with a caveat:

The same community can also be intrusive. Dr. Weiss describes standing at a party, drink in hand, when someone asks what kind of cancer you had, what you did, and whether it came back. Her advice to patients, which she took herself: “Put up your hand and say, ‘thank you so much for caring, but I cannot hear another story right now.’”

On the topic of AI and its impact on treatment and care, Dr. Weiss is cautiously optimistic. On the treatment front, she points to tools that help radiologists read mammograms more thoroughly and assess future risk as game changers in the fight against breast cancer.

Breastcancer.org also uses AI for tasks such as finding citations and interpreting pathology reports. But like many, she is wary of misinformation. “When you’re fearful, you look for reassurance, and you don’t want to be reassured by misinformation. When it comes to health information, every word matters.”

Her final advice is for the appointment itself, which she says she has even struggled with. “When they start speaking quickly in complex medical language, you can get lost really fast. The risk is you kind of fake it. That must not happen.”

“Do your research in advance. Write things down. Bring someone you trust as a second set of ears. Ask direct questions. Don’t worry if it sounds funny or silly. It’s always a smart question when you are dealing with your health.” Just be prepared for the questions to multiply from there. “Once you get a certain set of questions answered, that raises more questions. So just write it all down.”

If breast cancer has touched your life, know that you are not alone. Healthline’s Bezzy Breast Cancer Community is a space for peer support, feel-good stories, and advice in a welcoming, stigma-free environment when your lived experience is seen, heard and valued.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Saturday in our Healthline Daily newsletter. He’ll soon be launching a dedicated Letter from the Editor newsletter coming to an inbox near you later in the fall.

#4744. BYD (BYDDY) Q3 profit jumps 28% on exports, but inventory balloons 60%

BYD’s Q3 2026 earnings are out, and net profit jumped 28% year-over-year to ¥10.02 billion as the Chinese automaker shipped more than half a million vehicles out of the country in just three months.

But the rest of the filing is messier. BYD’s inventory is up 60% since January, its cash pile has shrunk by almost half, and profit is still down for the first nine months of the year.

BYD is still operating at a high level, but its business is changing.

BYD filed its third-quarter report with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on Thursday. Here are the key figures for July through September:

That’s BYD’s best quarterly profit since the end of 2024, and the first time revenue has grown year-over-year after four straight quarters of declines.

It’s also a big rebound from the start of the year. BYD’s Q1 2026 profit collapsed 55% to ¥4.08 billion, before recovering to ¥8.24 billion in Q2.

Still, it came in under expectations. Brokerages polled by Reuters were looking for ¥11.4 billion to ¥12.95 billion.

And zoom out to the full year so far, and BYD is treading water. Revenue for the first nine months was ¥566.30 billion, up just 0.01%, while net profit fell 4.2% to ¥22.34 billion. That’s on top of 2025, when BYD’s annual profit had already dropped to ¥32.62 billion from ¥40.25 billion in 2024.

The quarterly report doesn’t break out vehicle volumes, but BYD’s monthly sales filings do. The automaker sold 1,323,065 vehicles in Q3, up 18.7% from 1,114,192 a year earlier.

All of that growth, and then some, came from outside China. BYD exported 550,704 vehicles in the quarter, up 137% from 232,806 in Q3 2025. Everything else, which is mostly the Chinese market, fell about 12% to roughly 772,000 units.

Exports now account for 42% of BYD’s sales. In the first half, overseas markets already brought in ¥181.3 billion, or 53% of the company’s revenue.

For perspective, Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles worldwide in Q3. BYD exported more cars than Tesla sold on the entire planet.

At home, it’s a different story. China’s price war hasn’t let up, and BYD is now fighting it with cars like the new Seagull with 5-minute flash charging, starting under $10,000. That’s great for buyers. Not so much for margins.

BYD doesn’t report gross margin in its quarterly filing, but it can be calculated from the income statement. We get about 18.0% for Q3, slightly better than 17.6% a year ago, but down from roughly 18.9% in Q2.

The bigger hits are further down the income statement.

Finance expenses came in at ¥7.37 billion for the first nine months, compared to a ¥2.94 billion gain in the same period last year. BYD blames exchange losses. That’s a swing of more than ¥10 billion when the company made ¥22.34 billion in profit, which is the price of doing half your business in foreign currencies.

Impairment charges are also climbing. BYD booked ¥2.71 billion in asset impairment losses, up 68%, which it says is mostly inventory write-downs because of “the expanded inventory scale.” Credit losses tripled to ¥944 million, set aside “in line with the increase in trade receivables.”

And then there’s R&D. BYD’s research and development expenses fell 17% to ¥36.28 billion over nine months. A small part of that is accounting, since BYD capitalized more development costs on its balance sheet this year, but it’s still a notable drop for a company that has built its brand on vertical integration and in-house tech.

Here’s how a few key line items moved between Dec. 31, 2025 and Sept. 30, 2026:

BYD attributes both the inventory and receivables jumps “mainly” to the growth of its overseas auto business. That makes sense. Cars on ships, in ports and at foreign dealers sit on the books a lot longer than a car sold to a dealer in China.

The bills payable number stands out too. Those are short-term notes BYD hands suppliers instead of cash, and they more than tripled this year, which BYD explains as “the increase in settlement of bills.”

On the financing side, BYD cut its short-term bank borrowings roughly in half to ¥18.67 billion, but tripled its bonds outstanding to ¥14.99 billion and issued super short-term commercial paper.

To be fair, there are healthy signals in there as well. Operating cash flow for the first nine months was ¥54.47 billion, up 33%. Customer prepayments (contract liabilities) rose 81% to ¥92.95 billion, which points to strong orders. And cash spent on new factories and equipment fell 24% to ¥87.38 billion as BYD’s huge buildout slows down.

On the surface, this is a good quarter for BYD. Profit is up 28%, revenue is growing again, and the export strategy is clearly working. BYD exporting more cars in a quarter than Tesla sells worldwide would have sounded absurd just three years ago.

But we don’t think it’s as clean as the headline number suggests.

BYD had a rocket like ascension and sales exploded while they kept on introducing better technology. Considering the competition increase, they are still doing very well. They are not even everywhere yet but that is probably coming at some point soon too.

BYD added over ¥83 billion worth of inventory in nine months while its sales were down 3.9% year-to-date. Receivables are up, supplier IOUs are up, and cash is way down. That’s what it looks like when you push a lot of cars into a long overseas pipeline and wait to get paid for them. It works as long as those cars sell at decent prices. If they don’t, those impairment charges we’re already seeing get a lot bigger.

And the domestic business isn’t getting easier. BYD is selling fewer cars in China than a year ago while it now employs over 1 million people. The cuts to R&D spending are a sign the company is looking for savings somewhere.

These are all signs of BYD’s business changing. It is going to take a while for it to settle, but I think they are currently in a great spot with the switch to their Blade battery 2.0 virtually over, and new capacity coming from Hungary, Thailand, and Brazil.

#4743. Women With Autoimmune Diseases More Likely to Be Misdiagnosed Than Men

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new international study found that women with autoimmune diseases often experience longer delays in getting a correct diagnosis compared to men.

The research, published in eClinicalMedicine on October 12, also shows that females report higher rates of being misdiagnosed, especially with mental health or psychosomatic conditions.

These findings highlight challenges in diagnosing autoimmune diseases and suggest that sex differences affect patients’ experiences in healthcare.

This is significant given that autoimmune diseases, conditions in which the body’s immune system attacks its own healthy cells, are estimated to affect around 4.6% of the U.S. population. Additionally, despite the observed disparities in diagnoses, women are almost two times as likely as men to be diagnosed with an autoimmune disease.

Researchers conducted an online survey between December 7, 2024, and March 7, 2025, inviting adults ages 18 and older who had a confirmed autoimmune or rheumatic disease.

The survey was carefully designed and tested with input from patients, charities, and medical experts to ensure it captured important information about patients’ diagnostic journeys.

Participants were asked about the time it took from when they first noticed symptoms to when they received their autoimmune diagnosis.

They also reported how many healthcare visits they made before diagnosis and whether they felt their symptoms were ever misdiagnosed as mental health issues, psychosomatic problems (physical symptoms caused or worsened by psychological factors), or another physical disease.

The survey was widely shared on social media, patient support groups, and community organizations to reach a broad audience.

Special efforts were made to include underrepresented groups such as males, younger individuals, and people from minority ethnic backgrounds.

The survey was available in five languages, and participants could complete it with help from researchers if needed.

To analyze the data, the team used statistical methods, adjusting for factors like age, type of autoimmune disease, continent of residence, and financial situation.

These methods helped compare the experiences of males and females while accounting for differences in disease types and other factors

The study included 6,607 participants, with 91.2% identifying as female and most living in the United Kingdom. On average, women were younger than men in the study.

Autoimmune thyroid disease was the most common condition reported. Non-autoimmune conditions like anxiety were more commonly reported by women, while men reported higher rates of hypertension.

One of the main findings was that women reported longer delays before getting a diagnosis. Nearly 32% of females experienced delays of four years or more from symptom onset to diagnosis, compared to about 26% of males.

On the other hand, men were more likely to be diagnosed within a year of symptom onset (nearly 50% of males versus 40% of females).

Women also made more visits to healthcare providers before diagnosis, with 26.2% having 11 or more visits compared to 18.4% of men.

When it came to misdiagnoses, women were significantly more likely to report that their symptoms had been mistaken for mental health issues (43.3% of females vs. 32.7% of males) or psychosomatic causes (33.9% of females vs. 21.5% of males).

However, there was no significant difference between men and women in being misdiagnosed with another physical disease.

The type of autoimmune disease also influenced misdiagnosis rates. Diseases with clear physical symptoms or definitive lab tests, like type 1 diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, had lower rates of mental health and psychosomatic misdiagnoses.

In contrast, conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis or undifferentiated connective tissue disease had higher rates of these misdiagnoses (over 50%).

After adjusting for disease type and other factors, women still had higher odds of reporting mental health or psychosomatic misdiagnoses compared to men.

Other factors affected misdiagnosis rates, too. People living in continents outside the United Kingdom, those with lower household income, and certain disease groups were more likely to report psychiatric or psychosomatic misdiagnoses. Age, however, was not linked to the risk of being misdiagnosed.

Muhammad Qasim, MD, a pulmonologist and medical writer with MySleepApneaTeam, told Healthline that autoimmune diseases are often difficult to diagnose. Qasim wasn’t involved in the study.

“Early symptoms can be vague, fluctuate over time, and affect several parts of the body,” he said. “Fatigue, pain, sleep problems, brain fog, and mood changes do not immediately point to one diagnosis.”

Qasim echoed the study’s findings, explaining that similar symptoms may be interpreted differently in women versus men, with complaints being attributed to anxiety, stress, or psychosomatic causes.

However, there are probably multiple factors contributing to this phenomenon, he said.

“Differences in disease presentation, gaps in research, fragmented care, and unconscious bias can all contribute,” said Qasim. “Once a psychiatric explanation enters the medical record, there is also a risk that later clinicians view new symptoms through that same lens.”

Regarding unconscious bias, the study’s authors noted that women have historically been treated by doctors as “less credible” and more “emotional” in reporting their symptoms, which can influence how doctors interpret them.

These disparities in diagnosis are important, however, because longer waits and erroneous diagnoses can delay proper treatment and increase women’s frustration, leading them to stop asking for help.

The researchers suggest that healthcare providers need to be aware of these concerns and consider autoimmune diseases carefully when patients, especially females, present with more complicated symptoms.

Adam Carewe, MD, a physician in Boulder, CO, and a clinical informaticist with General Medicine who wasn’t involved in the study, offered guidance to those experiencing symptoms on how to obtain a proper diagnosis.

Healthgrades is owned by RVO Health. By clicking on this link, we may receive a commission. Learn more.

“Patients can keep an accurate symptom timeline, bring in family history, ask what else could be explaining these symptoms, ask for a plan for next steps if initial testing/treatment, do not change anything, and lastly get a second opinion,” he advised.

Carewe emphasized the value of not giving up on finding answers. “The most important thing for anyone with persistent symptoms of any kind is to continue to work with your primary care clinician and continue to advocate for yourself,” he said.

#4742. The Inner Voice Isn't Always the Inner Enemy

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 8, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

For a long time, I felt like an imposter. Although I had graduated from medical school, passed the internal medicine boards, and completed a residency, part of me still grappled with imposter syndrome.

Imposter syndrome (also called the impostor phenomenon) is when you persistently doubt your abilities, feel like a fraud, and fear others will expose you, even when you have clear proof of your success.

I suppose it had to do with my early childhood. I was molested from the ages of 11 to 13. I told my parents, but when they confronted the senior Boy Scout leaders, they were shamed into silence. I was left with an undying feeling that it was all my fault. I internalized this, and that gave birth to a voice inside my head that wasn’t my own. It belonged to my perpetrator, who installed it in me when I didn’t have the language to refute it.

While I engaged with several therapists over decades, I foolishly believed that the shame I was attempting to overcome was something I could outrun, suppress, or avoid. And for a while, I believed I had. The proof was clear: I became a married physician. I was successful, and yet when the COVID-19 pandemic hit, all the pillars that had quietly moored me to my external life disappeared. In that isolation, shame came roaring back.

I, like millions of Americans, ran to alcohol to cope.

Throughout this period, the voice inside my head, the one I dubbed the unreliable narrator, played on an endless loop. He told me that I was too much, or not enough, or fundamentally broken. I believed him because, well, he was the voice in my head. I was ill-equipped to challenge this voice or ask whether these were facts or simply thoughts. It never occurred to me because that voice lived so clearly inside me that challenging him meant challenging the very framework that had made me a success.

This conflict became apparent when my beloved manager, an Ivy League professor, called me idiotic. No, he didn’t call me an idiot, though he might as well have. He said "idiotic," and I internalized that word and shut down. I couldn’t speak. I couldn't breathe. It was a truly embarrassing experience.

Eventually, I recovered, but I sat with that moment for a long time. What I came to understand much later was that, by using the term idiotic, my beloved manager activated an old trauma I had locked away in my subconscious. My former child molester often called me an idiot. When my manager used that word in a conversation with my adult self, it triggered a trauma response in my younger self—fight, flight, or freeze. My body chose freeze.

What I learned from this experience is the power of the pause—pausing is your superpower. Far too many of us respond quickly, often talking before the other person has finished their sentence. But I took it a step further and developed the four P’s: pause, present, ponder, and possibilities.

The trick is you have to practice when you’re not activated. Next time you’re speaking to your friend, when they stop talking, don’t answer. Pause. Count to three, check in with yourself, be present, ponder the situation, and then, and only then, can you see the possibilities.

Internal self: “What’s going on with you now?”

Activated self: “I'm feeling my face flush. My heart is racing.”

Internal self: “Okay, you’re experiencing shame. Do you have any idea why?"

Activated self: “My child molester used to call me an idiot.”

Internal self: “Okay, but you’re not an idiot. In fact, you’re not 11 years old. You’re an adult doctor, and this situation has nothing to do with what happened to you decades ago."

Internal self: “Now that you understand your manager activated some old trauma, how would you like to respond?"

Activated self: “You asked a good question. It deserves some thought. Let me get back to you.”

Remember: You can't think your way out of shame that lives in your nervous system.

Shame is a well-intentioned guard dog with terrible judgment about what constitutes actual danger.

Spinelli, F. (2026). The shame compass: A radical framework for trauma healing and self-acceptance. Level Best Books.

Clance, P. R., & Imes, S. A. (1978). The imposter phenomenon in high achieving women: Dynamics and therapeutic intervention. Psychotherapy: Theory, Research & Practice, 15(3), 241–247.

van der Kolk, B. A. (2014). The body keeps the score: Brain, mind, and body in the healing of trauma. Viking.

#4741. The Ford Escape may return as an EV based on the UEV platform [Update]

Ford pulled the plug on the Escape last year after a 25-year run, but the crossover SUV could return as an EV on the new UEV platform.

While Ford is preparing to launch the Fathom, its first vehicle based on the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform in 2027, the company is already hinting at what could be its second UEV-based model.

The last gas-powered Escape models rolled off the production line at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant as it retooled the facility to prepare for the new Fathom electric pickup.

Typically, when Ford retires a model, its landing page says something like “we’re discontinuing” it, or “it’s the end of the road,” such as with the Edge SUV.

Meanwhile, the Escape landing page says the “SUV may be taking a breather for now,” declaring the “Ford Escape is tapping the brakes,” with no mention of it being discontinued. Instead, the site directs you to check out Ford’s other vehicles while it’s on hiatus.

According to Ford Authority, the Escape will return as an all-electric crossover SUV based on the UEV platform.

Update 10/29/2026: A Ford spokesperson told Electrek that the Ford Authority report is pure speculation and the company has not announced the Escape will return as an EV or that it will be based on the UEV platform.

If it does come to life, the Ford Escape EV would likely remain close in size to the outgoing gas model, which measures 180.1″ long, 74.1″ wide (without mirrors), and 66.1″ tall, with a 106.7″ wheelbase. That’s about the size of other compact SUVs like the Toyota RAV4 and Hyundai Tucson.

The report claimed the electric Escape is expected to enter production at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in 2029, possibly making it the second vehicle based on its UEV platform, following the Fathom pickup.

CEO Jim Farley confirmed on Ford’s Q3 earnings call on Wednesday that the Fathom launch “remains on track for the fourth quarter of next year.”

The Fathom is “a breakthrough product,” Farley said, adding the pickup is highly capable, innovative, and affordable.

Ford will open preorders for the Fathom in early 2027, starting at $28,350 for the standard-range version. With the $1,595 delivery fee, Ford’s electric pickup will still start under $30,000, which the company says will be “right in the heart of the market.”

The Fathom will be the first vehicle to integrate Apple Maps into its navigation system. It will also be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving. Other standard features include Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, plus bidirectional charging capabilities.

Ford claims the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, not including the added bed and frunk (front trunk).

2029 seems a little slow, but I'm glad Ford is still pushing ahead with EV plans.

Inside, the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with an easy-to-use navigation system using Apple Maps.

Ford has yet to reveal battery specs or range, but the UEV platform uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to reduce costs. We also know the Fathom will have an NACS charge port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

The UEV platform is flexible enough to underpin vehicles ranging from compact crossovers to pickup trucks and vans, so an electric Escape would make sense.

With the Fathom set to launch next year, we should learn more about the potential Ford Escape EV soon. Check back for updates.
